newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Lion rebuilds strength after shakeout.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lion rebuilds strength after shakeout.

text.p: Australasian brewer Lion Nathan Ltd's chief executive Douglas Myers said on Monday management had become leaner since the departure of several key personnel last year and it had improved its market contact as a result.
Myers told Reuters in an interview the New Zealand-based brewer had also gained market share in Australia in the last two months while its position in its home market had stabilised.
In the key Australian beer market, where 70 percent of its assets are tied up, Lion last year reported a drop in market share to 42 percent from 43.4 percent.
It had the leading market share in three of the country's five states, however, and Myers said, "in the last couple of months it's actually become a bit stronger (in Australia)".
At the same time as its position improved across the Tasman, he called its performance in New Zealand "stable".

Lion has struggled against the tide of shrinking sales in recent months, and it soft share performance has reflected analysts' expectation that profits will not match last year's net profit of NZ$91.2 million.
It is due to report half-year results later this month.
Myers said that the shakeout in management had resulted in him adopting a more "hands on" approach as chief executive.

Observers could have been forgiven for thinking Lion had a revolving door policy with its top staff, culminating in the widely-publicised departure of chief operating officer Kevin Roberts late last year. He was not replaced.
"It became apparent to both Kevin and us that what we needed and what we wanted to do was not the same thing," Myers said.

"It has made me a lot closer to what's going on in the business because previously there was a guy in between, so now I've got direct contact with the four trading companies. It's created a lot of velocity and the removal of a barrier."
There had been a general flattening of structures right through the company, not just on the corporate level, he added.
In Australia, where Lion acquired the brewing assets of the now defunct Bond Corp, the challenge had been to form a national company from an amalgam of regional brewers.
Lion now has Gordon Cairns as chief operating officer in Australia. Under Cairns, Myers believes Lion had struck the right balance between central and regional control.
The accent had also turned to more advertising and less sponsorship, with increased focus on its core brands.
Now that the structure had settled, Myers said Lion's brands were in better shape, helping the improvement in its Australian market share.
"In this last quarter we've been doing better and I'm quite pleased with that, because we have gone through Kevin's departure, the appointment of Gordon, and the total restructuring of the company.
"There has been a lot going on and to have been able to do that and see a strengthening of market share is pretty positive," Myers said.

In China, construction of Lion's new brewery at Souzhou was ahead of schedule, under budget and due for completion in October, he said. Lion expects Souzhou to turn to profit within two or three years.
In the year to August, Lion's Chinese joint venture operation at Wuxi made an operating profit of NZ$2.3 million,
Lion has been seeking another opportunity of similar size to Wuxi but Myers said the issue had become complex. For the time being, the focus was still on getting Souzhou up and running.
Operating in China meant the company had to develop a style of management that was suitable for the local business environment. Lion has about NZ$300 million invested in China.
--Wellington Newsroom 64-4 4734 746
